text: Noninvasive DNA sampling from scats can provide powerful tools for wildlife research depending in large part on how scats are collected in the field. Preservation of scat in 95-100% ethanol can be highly effective, but not always practical. Use of swabs to sample the mucous layer from scats is a popular alternative, but has not been adequately tested in arid environments, where the mucous layer can rapidly desiccate. We conducted a paired comparison of methods, extraction from scats stored in ethanol ("direct method") versus from swabs ("swab method"), for carnivore scats collected under typical field conditions during May-September 2013 and January-February 2015 in northern California, USA. Direct quantification of DNA indicated that the extracts from ethanol-preserved direct-method samples contained, on average, an order of magnitude (14Â) more target DNA than extracts from swab method (P < 0.03). For mitochondrial sequencing, which is typically used for species-typing, we obtained slightly higher success for the direct (81%) than the swab (73%) extracts, but not significantly so (P ¼ 0.25, n ¼ 104). Among 62 canid scats, microsatellite genotyping (typically used for individual identification) was much more successful for the direct extracts (74%) than the swab extracts (35%; P < 0.001, n ¼ 62). Together, our findings indicated a substantial advantage of ethanol preservation followed by extraction directly from scats over swabbing in our arid study area. Our results apply most specifically to canids in the arid study environment; swabbing is potentially more effective in humid environments or in other carnivore species. Nevertheless, our findings highlight the importance of conducting pilot studies before committing to swabbing as a means of fecal DNA collection.

Noninvasive fecal sampling and genetic analyses of scats are used increasingly in wildlife research (e.g., Waits and Paetkau 2005, Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, Gulsby et al. 2015, Lounsberry et al. 2015). The value of this approach for estimating abundance, occupancy, individual longevity, home range, habitat use, gene flow, and social structure without the need to capture or handle individual animals presents tremendous potential, but applications are often limited by challenges in adequately preserving samples for subsequent DNA extraction and analyses (e.g., Schwartz et al. 2007).
Although many variables (e.g., diet, environmental conditions, time since deposition, DNA extraction method) can affect the success of DNA acquisition from scats (Waits and Paetkau 2005), the single most influential factor in control of most field biologists is how samples are collected and stored prior to transfer to a laboratory. A variety of storage methods have been used and tested for efficacy, including desiccation, freezing, or storage in buffers or ethanol. In most studies, pure ethanol (i.e., 95-100%) works similarly to or better than other methods for shorter storage periods and can substantially outperform them during extended storage periods (Murphy et al. 2002, Frantz et al. 2003, Piggott and Taylor 2003, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009, Panasci et al. 2011, Tende et al. 2014). However, acquiring, storing, and transporting sufficient quantities of ethanol for sample storage can be difficult in remote field conditions. Sample transport following collection and storage can also pose an issue because ethanol is volatile, highly flammable, and is subject to various shipping and travel restrictions (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). One alternative has been to use dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-based buffers such as DET (e.g., Panasci et al. 2011, Vynne et al. 2011), but this method has a limited shelf-life relative to ethanol (e.g., Murphy et al. 2002).
Another method that has become increasingly popular, and is even required by some service laboratories, involves the use of a cotton swab to collect the epithelial cells themselves from the mucous layer of scats in the field (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). The accessibility of the mucous layer, however, likely depends on time in the environment, ambient conditions, and various other factors. In general, fecal swabs are likely to be most successful when scats are sufficiently fresh that the mucous layer containing the epithelial cells remains moist, also enabling separation from the fecal matrix, which typically contains polymerase chain reaction (PCR) inhibitors (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009). Depending on the purpose of a study, however, reliance solely on freshly deposited scats may not be feasible, such as in studies of rare species (e.g., Stenglein et al. 2010, Sacks et al. 2011, Statham et al. 2012, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). Therefore, it is of interest to know how methods of fecal collection and preservation are likely to perform relative to one another under more variable field conditions. In such cases, the mucous layer may not be as readily separated from the external scat via swabbing.
Unfortunately, it is difficult to evaluate the efficacy of swabs used on nonfresh scats based on the existing literature because few studies have reported their success in terms of DNA quantity (but see Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009), which, along with PCR inhibition, ultimately determines all measures of downstream success. Comparisons based solely on the downstream success measures themselves, such as proportion of scats that yield species types, are complicated by differences among study protocols. This problem is particularly significant for nuclear DNA (nDNA) amplification, which can be highly sensitive to particular species, markers, amplification protocols, and the authors' criteria for success (e.g., number of loci amplifying, differences in numbers of replication attempts, etc.). For these reasons, paired comparisons are crucial. We are aware of only one such study (i.e., using scats of unknown and variable ages), which compared extractions from swabs of scats preserved by freezing (i.e., swabbed in the laboratory at the time of extraction) to those from subsamples of the same scats preserved in DMSO buffer (Vynne et al. 2011). The study reported a 73% success rate in mitochondrial amplification of the swab extracts, which was higher than the comparably low 53% success they achieved for the DMSO-based extracts. Nevertheless, genotyping success from those swab samples identified in the first step to be from the target species was relatively high (82%). However, this study was conducted in a semitropical climate, which potentially preserves the moisture in the mucous layer for a greater period of time. We are aware of no study that has compared swabbing directly to ethanol-preserved scats or which has explored the efficacy of swabbing in an arid environment. In the present study, we used a paired design to directly compare the performance of methods involving fecal swabs versus ethanol-preserved fecal material using mesocarnivore scats collected from an arid, Mediterranean climate zone, and ranging up to 3 weeks old. We compared approaches both in terms of mitochondrial DNA sequencing, which is commonly used for species identification, and, for a subset of scats that were shown to be canine, nuclear (e.g., microsatellite) genotyping, which is used for individual and sex identification. Importantly, we also directly quantified the amount of target-species DNA in extracts, which will facilitate future comparisons to studies in other environments.

We collected scats for this study from California's Sacramento Valley (USA), in elevations <150 m, latitudes ranging from 39.368N to 40.408N, and longitudes ranging from 122.258W to 121.438W. The landscape was composed primarily of agricultural lands, including flooded rice agriculture, dry cropland, vineyards, and orchards. Remnant grasslands remained where livestock were grazed. The study area was hot (highs ranged from 328 C to 408 C) and experienced almost no precipitation during the summer, and mild (highs ranged from 88 C to 248 C), with very little precipitation during the particular winter during which sampling for this study was conducted.

We collected 104 putative mesocarnivore scats for this study during May-September 2013 (n ¼ 79) and January-February 2015 (n ¼ 25). We resampled transects every 2-3 weeks, collecting all mesocarnivore scats encountered. The 104 scats used for this study excluded those collected on the first run of transects and, therefore, were presumed to have been collected 21 days since deposition. In the field, we collected scats in individually labeled paper sacks and recorded whether scats appeared fresh (<2 days old), moderate-aged (2-4 days old), or older (>4 days). Within 12 hr of collection, we transferred a portion of each scat (approx. 2 g) into >4 parts (approx. 8-12 mL) 95-100% ethanol in a 15-mL tube and swabbed the unsampled portion of the same scat. Specifically, we used Q-tips 1 cotton-tipped swabs to sample the external surface area of approximately half of each scat on all sides. We first moistened swabs with 95-100% ethanol to help free cells from the scat surface (except for 3 scats that were so fresh there was no need to premoisten swabs; Rutledge et al. 2009). We allowed swabs to air dry and then stored them in manila coin envelopes. We stored all samples at room temperature (20-258 C) until DNA extraction. The average time between collection in the field and DNA extraction was 9.3 days (SD ¼ 7.7 days). Note: we chose ethanol as the moistening agent because it evaporates quickly. However, because other studies have moistened swabs with salt solutions, such as phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; e.g., DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), we swabbed a subset of 25 scats with both PBS and ethanol; we found no significant differences (Supporting Information 1). We also used a subset of samples to test our primary storage method (i.e., dried in manila envelopes) to storage of swabs in ethanol to control for the preservation versus the celltransfer aspect of swabbing and, again, found no qualitative differences in terms of DNA yield, inhibition, or performance (Supporting Information 2).
For DNA extraction directly from the ethanol-preserved scat samples, we used a QIAmp Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) to extract DNA from approximately 200 mg of the outer surface of scats, following the manufacturer's protocol, except that DNA was eluted in 100 mL of elution buffer. For swab samples, we extracted DNA using a DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen). We transferred swabs from envelopes directly into 2-mL microcentrifuge tubes with reagents for digestion: 700 mL PBS, 200 mL of Buffer AL, and 25 mL of Proteinase K. To remove swabs from the digestion tubes, we vortexed samples for 5-10 s, centrifuged them for 1 min at 14,000 rpm, and pressed swabs against the sides of the tubes to remove any remaining liquid before discarding. All subsequent steps followed manufacturer's instructions. Hereafter, we use the terms "direct" and "swab" to differentiate the DNA extracted directly from scat preserved in ethanol versus from swabs, respectively. We first attempted to amplify and sequence a 402-bp fragment of the mammalian mitochondrial cytochrome b gene using primers (Perrine et al. 2007) and procedures (Aubry et al. 2009) described previously. Although use of a shorter fragment, such as by other studies (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011;DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), would likely have produced higher species-typing success, we chose the longer fragment for purposes specific to various ongoing research projects in our laboratory. Because the direct method typically incorporates some fecal matrix in the extraction procedure, these extracts were likely to contain PCR inhibitors. Therefore, for direct-method extracts failing to amplify in the first step, we performed 10-fold dilutions to reduce the concentration of any PCR inhibitors and attempted a second time to amplify them at the cytochrome b fragment (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). (We did not sequence the samples that amplified after dilution, which resulted in 4 samples that amplified but which we did not species-type or, therefore, use in subsequent analyses.) We evaluated sequences to determine species using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) in the nucleotide database in Genbank.
From the scats that assigned to coyote (Canis latrans), gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), or red fox (Vulpes vulpes) for !1 of the 2 preservation methods in the previous step, we selected all but 10 samples (set aside for unrelated purposes) to attempt nDNA amplification. Specifically, we attempted to amplify 7 canine nuclear DNA microsatellite loci that amplify in all canid species in our study area (AHT137, AHT142, CXX-279, CXX-374, INU055, REN162C04, REN169O18; primer sequences provided by Moore et al. 2010). Because nuclear DNA occurs in much lower copy-number than mitochondrial DNA, we used only the undiluted (i.e., original) extracts, along with the Qiagen Multiplex PCR Kit reagents and manufacturer's protocol using Q-solution (Sacks et al. 2011). We used STRand software to call alleles (Toonen and Hughes 2001). Because we were primarily interested in gross performance, we did not attempt to quantify allelic dropout, which would have required replications, but instead report numbers of loci amplified and, for purposes of quantifying success discretely, considered genotyping successful when !6 loci were successfully amplified for at least one allele in the single attempt. Elsewhere, we have reported allelic dropout rates for the same study system using the direct-method approach (Sacks et al. 2010(Sacks et al. , 2011)).
Lastly, we performed a quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of a subset of 35 pairs of the undiluted extracts on which we attempted genotyping. The reduced subset was necessary to complete the quantitation assay on a single 96-well plate, which also included 12 internal positive control (IPC) standards, 12 extracts used in the supplementary swab-storage comparison (Supporting Information 2), and 2 blanks. We estimated concentration of canine genomic DNA based on canine Melanocortin-1 receptor gene copies and incorporated the IPC (a synthetic DNA fragment added to each sample in known concentration) for detection of PCR inhibition (Evans et al. 2007). We quantified inhibition in terms of the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to a predetermined threshold concentration minus the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to the same threshold concentration in standards containing no inhibitors; specifically, we used the average value among 12 standards. We incorporated negative controls into all procedures, including extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing, and genotyping steps. Importantly, our technique quantified canine genomic DNA only, whereas previous studies (Rutledge et al. 2009) quantified total genomic DNA, which includes up to 20Â as much nontarget (e.g., from intestinal microorganisms) as target DNA (Ball et al. 2007).
For each fecal extraction protocol, we calculated success rates in terms of species identification, genotyping success, and both processes combined. We compared methods with respect to numbers of mitochondrial DNA amplifications and failures and microsatellite successes and failures using Fisher's exact tests (Zar 1999). We compared microsatellite genotyping success across species using a x 2 test of independence (Zar 1999). Because the cutoff for genotyping success was necessarily arbitrary, we also used a 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate the effects of method and species on numbers of loci amplified (including zeros) in the canid scats. We used paired t-tests to compare DNA concentrations and inhibition between the direct and swab methods. We log-transformed the DNA concentration estimates prior to analysis to normalize residuals. To estimate 95% confidence intervals for proportions (or percentages), we employed a method based on the F-distribution (Zar 1999). Statistical tests were run using SYSTAT (version 9.0, SPSS Incorporated, Chicago, IL) and significance was assessed at alpha ¼ 0.05.

We amplified mitochondrial DNA successfully from 84 (80.8%, 95% CI ¼ 71.9-87.8%) of the 104 samples using the direct method compared with 76 (73.1%, 95% CI ¼ 63.5-81.3%) using the swab method (Table 1). This difference was not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, P ¼ 0.25). We observed little difference in success rates for scats thought to be <2 days old versus those apparently 2-4 days old, but a marked decline in success in the oldest-looking scats (Fig. 1). Altogether, we obtained at least one amplification product from 91 of the 104 scats. A BLAST search indicated 72 of the 87 scats were from one of the 3 wild-canine target species (Table 1).
For microsatellite genotyping, we obtained significantly greater success using the direct-extracts (74.2%, 95% CI ¼ 61.5-84.5%) compared with the swab extracts (35.5%, 95% CI ¼ 23.7-48.7%; Fisher's exact test, P < 0.001), and significantly greater success for red fox scats than for coyote or gray fox scats for both the direct method (89.5% [95% CI ¼ 75.2-97.1%] red fox, 50.0% [95% CI ¼ 29.1-70.9%] coyote and gray fox; x 2 2 ¼ 12.0, P ¼ 0.003) and the swab method (47.4% [95% CI ¼ 31.0-64.2%] red fox, 16.7% [95% CI ¼ 4.7-37.4%] coyote and gray fox; x 2 1;2 ¼ 6.1, P ¼ 0.048). Although we considered our single attempt successful only if !6 loci amplified on the initial attempt, replicate genotyping could have increased our success for both direct and swab extracts. For example, we amplified !1 locus in 42 of the 64 canid scats from swabs, suggesting that we could have potentially increased our swab genotyping success to a maximum of 66% (i.e., if all of these produced usable genotypes after multiple attempts), albeit with significant added expense. We also amplified significantly more of the 7 microsatellite loci using the direct extracts ( x ¼ 5.7 loci, SE ¼ 0.27) compared with the swab extracts ( x ¼ 3.1 loci, SE ¼ 0.38; ANOVA: F 1,118 ¼ 27.5, P < 0.001), and obtained a significantly greater success rate for both methods, respectively, for red fox scats ( x ¼ 6.4 vs. 4.2 loci) than for coyote ( x ¼ 4.6 vs. 1.4 loci) or gray fox ( x ¼ 4.5 vs. 1.2 loci) scats (F 2,118 ¼ 14.5, P < 0.001). There was no significant interaction between method and species (F 2,118 ¼ 0.555, P ¼ 0.58), suggesting that differences in methods were qualitatively applicable to all 3 canid species investigated in this study, even though the success rates differed markedly among them. We performed qPCR on 35 of the canine samples. The DNA concentrations were much higher on average in the direct-method extracts ( x ¼ 0.85 ng/mL, SE ¼ 0.49 ng/mL) than the swab extracts ( x ¼ 0.06 ng/mL, SE ¼ 0.04 ng/mL; t 34 ¼ 2.28, P ¼ 0.029). However, inhibition also was much higher on average in the direct-method extracts ( x ¼ 2.01 cycles, SE ¼ 0.51 cycles) than the swab extracts ( x ¼ 0.07 cycles, SE ¼ 0.04 cycles; t 34 ¼ 3.63, P ¼ 0.001). To interpret inhibition values, we compared these to internal standards  (positive controls): the number of cycles required to reach threshold concentration in the absence of inhibition among these controls was 27.15 cycles (SD ¼ 0.43). Thus, relative to variation in the uninhibited controls, we identified 28.1 cycles (i.e., 27.15 þ 1.96 Â 0.43) as the lower limit for significant inhibition. We observed significant inhibition in only 1 swab extract (28.34 cycles) but in 15 of the directmethod extracts (range ¼ 28.12-38.05 cycles).

Previous studies have investigated the use of swabs to obtain DNA from epithelial cells on the periphery of very recently deposited scats (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009) or scats from boreal regions during winter when they were immediately frozen (Wasser et al. 2011). However, in many circumstances, dependence on fresh (or frozen) scats can be overly restrictive (e.g., Stenglein et al. 2010, Sacks et al. 2011, Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b).
Studies in tropical regions have used swabs to obtain cells from older scats with some success (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). However, we are aware of no study prior to ours that has investigated the efficacy of swabs used to sample scats in an arid climate, where the mucous layer could desiccate more rapidly and, therefore, become more difficult to separate from the scat surface. For this reason, we conducted the present study to determine the efficacy of swabs to sample scats in an arid climate zone.
Our success rates for mitochondrial amplification and red fox scat genotyping of DNA extracted directly from scats collected in 95-100% ethanol were very similar to previous results using this same method in the same study area (Sacks et al. 2011). Specifically, based on 950 putative red fox scats, we had previously experienced an 84% success rate for mitochondrial amplification and an 82% microsatellite genotyping success rate (from 690 verified red fox scats; Sacks et al. 2011). In contrast, using swabs in this study, we achieved significantly lower sequencing success and, especially, genotyping success rates. Our genotyping success rates for coyotes and gray foxes paralleled these results, with genotyping success higher in both cases for the direct approach in comparison to swabbing. Reasons for the generally higher success rate in red foxes than the other 2 canid species were unclear. One possibility relates to the markers themselves, which were previously optimized specifically for red foxes (Moore et al. 2010). Alternatively, the differential success among species could stem from differences in DNA quantity or quality associated with scat extractions, for example, related to inhibitors associated with differing dietary tendencies. Unfortunately, we quantified DNA and tested for inhibitors in too few coyote (and no gray fox) samples to determine whether there could have been a systematic difference in DNA yield or inhibition among species in this study. The question of species-specific differences in DNA yield and overall success clearly requires further study. On the other hand, our quantification of the amount of target species DNA in our extracts from direct and swab methods on each scat clearly demonstrated that our higher success in the ethanol (direct) relative to swab extracts was attributable to significantly higher (over an order of magnitude) DNA yields from the former than latter sample types. Importantly, our relatively poor swab success could not be attributed to the particulars of our protocol. There are nearly as many variations on swabbing protocols as there are studies that have used swabs. For example, some studies have swabbed previously frozen scats to transfer cells directly into digestion buffer at the time of DNA extraction (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011), stored swabs in empty vials that were subsequently frozen (DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), or stored swabs in DET buffer at room temperature (Rutledge et al. 2009). We tried multiple approaches for preservation and handling of swabs prior to extraction, all of which produced similar results in terms of both DNA yields and amplification and genotyping success. We also found no differences related to whether we used PBS or ethanol as a swab-moistening agent. Thus, the factor that limited our swab success was simply the amount of intact DNA that we were able to recover from the periphery of scats that were collected in our study area. Vigorously rubbing a swab moistened either with ethanol or PBS over a significant portion of a scat surface was typically unable to recover as much DNA as a small portion of that surface used directly in extractions, suggesting that once the mucous layer had desiccated, swabbing was an inefficient way of removing epithelial cells from the fecal surface.
The superior performance of the direct method relative to the swab method(s) occurred despite greater transfer of PCR inhibitors in the former than latter method. In fact, the swab samples contained essentially no PCR inhibition based on the internal positive controls, whereas the direct extracts tended frequently to exhibit detectable PCR inhibition. We were eventually able to counter PCR inhibition of mitochondrial DNA sequencing by dilution of the extracts. Interestingly, nearly all of the same undiluted direct extracts that failed mitochondrial PCR were successfully genotyped with microsatellites in their undiluted form despite the presence of inhibitors confirmed in a subset of these. This success was likely due to the particular PCR chemistry we used for microsatellites. Although our mitochondrial DNA reactions utilized a standard polymerase (Amplitaq; Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA), our microsatellite reactions utilized a commercially available kit (Qiagen Multiplex) with a hot-start polymerase and proprietary additives (Q-solution) found previously to perform well for fecal DNA (Luikart et al. 2008).
Although it seems clear from our findings that swabs performed poorly compared with the direct use of scats stored in ethanol in our study, it is important to note that the swabs did not fail entirely. Swabs potentially could be useful in some circumstances, particularly for speciestyping from mitochondrial DNA, which is much more plentiful than nuclear DNA. Additionally, increased DNA concentration from swab extracts could be achieved by eluting DNA in a smaller quantity of buffer, such as 50 mL, rather than the 200 mL used in the present study. It is also possible that the success of swabs varied according to taxon. In particular, our findings are most applicable to canid scats.
Previous studies using swabs for canids and felids in higher humidity tropical environments experienced somewhat higher genotyping success than we did for canids in our arid study area (Vynne et al. 2011;DeMatteo et al. 2014a). Although our swab species-typing success was similar to those by Vynne et al. (2011;73%)   et al. 2014a). This difference could relate to humidity. Although humidity is thought to degrade DNA generally (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011), it is also conceivable that humidity causes the mucous layer to remain more easily separated from the scat surface for longer periods of time, potentially enhancing the relative utility of swabs in tropical or subtropical relative to Mediterranean climate zones. On the other hand, it is also possible that the higher nDNA success in the tropical studies stemmed from more sensitive downstream procedures used in those studies rather than from higher DNA quantity in extracts. For example, we only performed a single extraction attempt versus 2 by DeMatteo et al. (2014a, b); we performed a single genotyping attempt versus up to 4 by Vynne et al. (2011) and up to 6 by DeMatteo et al. (2014a), and to count as "successful," we required that all but one locus amplify, compared with a single sex marker by Vynne et al. (2011) and amplification of all but 2 or 3 loci (depending on species) by DeMatteo et al. (2014a, b). The disparity between the number of swab samples showing amplification of any loci versus 6 or more loci in this study suggests that our success rate with swabs might have been more similar to these tropical studies had we replicated extraction attempts, genotyping efforts, or used less stringent criteria for "success."
Thus, although fecal swabs appear to present an excellent alternative to ethanol fecal storage and extraction methods for very fresh samples and can be potentially useful in tropical environments, our findings suggest that studies relying to a large extent on older scat samples, particularly of canids in arid environments, can potentially obtain substantively better data sets by collecting scat pieces in ethanol and extracting DNA directly from their external surfaces. Other methods, such as those involving silica to keep samples dry, also have been shown to work well in some but not all instances (e.g., Murphy et al. 2002). Given the potentially significant time, effort, and expense required to obtain scats from rare carnivores, we suggest that swab-based collection methods should be carefully tested against others in pilot studies prior to embarking on large collections reliant on swabs or any other particular method and, if possible, to include preservation in pure ethanol as one of the comparison groups.
